text:
This guide explains how UK competition law can apply to licences of technology rights such as patents, know-how, database rights and software.

This guide is intended as an overview of the issues that you will need to consider when you assess whether the technology transfer agreements that you enter into are competition law compliant. In particular, it provides a practical starting point for businesses and other organisations considering whether a technology transfer agreement may benefit from the Technology Transfer Block Exemption Order 2026, referred to in this guide as the TTBEO.

For detailed information about the TTBEO and the application of competition law to technology transfer agreements, businesses should refer to the CMA’s guidance on the application of the Chapter I prohibition in the Competition Act 1998 to technology transfer agreements (the CMA Technology Transfer Guidance).

This guide is not a substitute for legal advice, nor is the CMA Technology Transfer Guidance.

It will usually be necessary to seek legal advice about the application of the TTBEO and competition law to technology transfer agreements.

Read Part 1 of the CMA Technology Transfer Guidance for the purpose and scope of the guidance, and Part 2 for the relevant legal framework.

Roadmap: assessing a technology transfer agreement

When assessing whether a technology transfer agreement may benefit from the TTBEO, the main questions to consider are:

Scope: Is the agreement a technology transfer agreement covered by the TTBEO?

Competitor status: Are the parties competitors or non-competitors?

Markets and thresholds: What are the relevant product and technology markets? Are the applicable market share thresholds met (or in relation to technology markets are there sufficient independent competing technologies)?

Hardcore restrictions: Does the agreement contain any restriction that removes the benefit of the TTBEO from the whole agreement?

Excluded restrictions: Does it contain any restriction that must be assessed separately, even if the rest of the agreement benefits from the TTBEO?

Individual assessment: If the TTBEO does not apply, does the agreement comply with the Chapter I prohibition or meet the conditions for individual exemption?

Important terms

A technology transfer agreement is an agreement where one business (the licensor) allows another business (the licensee) to use technology rights to make goods or provide services.

Examples of technology rights for these purposes include:

patents

know-how (which essentially refers to commercial secrets that can be used to produce goods or provide services)

design rights

database rights

computer software

Technology pools are not covered by the TTBEO and are considered separately in the CMA Technology Transfer Guidance. Businesses considering participation in, or licensing through, a technology pool should consult the relevant section on technology pools in Part 11 of the Guidance.

How does competition law apply?

Competition law protects businesses and consumers from anti-competitive behaviour. It promotes competitive markets, including by helping to keep them open and ensuring a level playing field. Competitive markets in turn help to increase choice and improve price and quality. They also spur innovation, investment and productivity.

The main UK competition law provision relevant to technology transfer agreements is the Competition Act 1998 (CA98). The Chapter I prohibition in the CA98 prohibits agreements between businesses that prevent, restrict or distort competition in the UK. This can include agreements that limit how businesses compete on price, output, customers, markets or innovation.

The Chapter I prohibition may apply where an agreement is implemented in the UK or has substantial and foreseeable effects on trade in the UK.

If the Chapter I prohibition is infringed, the consequences can be serious:

the agreement, or the problematic restrictions, may be void and unenforceable

the CMA may impose significant financial penalties

customers, competitors or other affected parties may bring damages claims

Technology transfer agreements will often be pro-competitive because they help spread technology and encourage innovation through incentivising research and development.

However, the Chapter I prohibition can apply to technology transfer agreements.

Read Part 2 and Part 3 of the CMA Technology Transfer Guidance for more information about the Chapter I prohibition and the overall assessment of technology transfer agreements.

The TTBEO

An agreement that restricts competition may not infringe competition law if it is exempt from the Chapter I prohibition on the basis that it meets the legal conditions for exemption under section 9 of the CA98. In broad terms, the agreement must create benefits (for example, efficiencies or innovations in the production or supply of products), give consumers a fair share of those benefits, avoid unnecessary restrictions and not eliminate competition.

A block exemption makes this easier. Block exemptions apply to categories of agreement that are generally likely to satisfy the conditions of exemption from the Chapter I prohibition. If an agreement falls within the category of agreements covered by the block exemption and meets the block exemption’s conditions, it is automatically exempt from the Chapter I prohibition.

The TTBEO is the block exemption for technology transfer agreements. An agreement that satisfies all the conditions of the TTBEO will not infringe the Chapter I prohibition. The TTBEO therefore provides a safe harbour for agreements that meet its conditions. An agreement that does not benefit from the TTBEO is not necessarily unlawful and may still comply with competition law, but will require an individual assessment to check that it does not breach competition law.

To benefit fully from the block exemption, an agreement must be a technology transfer agreement for the purposes of the TTBEO, must meet the relevant market share conditions set out in the TTBEO and must not contain hardcore restrictions or excluded restrictions.

Main questions

Question Why it matters

Is this a technology transfer agreement for the purposes of the TTBEO? The agreement must involve one party allowing another to use technology rights (as defined in the TTBEO, which include patents, know-how, design rights, database rights and computer software) to make goods or provide services. This is important because, if the agreement is not a technology transfer agreement, it cannot benefit from the TTBEO. Note the TTBEO does not apply to agreements involving more than 2 parties.

Are the parties competitors? This affects the market share thresholds and the list of hardcore restrictions that apply to the agreement.

Are the applicable market share thresholds met? If not, the TTBEO may not apply, though the agreement may still be lawful - but it will require individual assessment.

Does the agreement contain a hardcore restriction? If yes, the whole agreement will lose the benefit of the TTBEO and is likely to infringe the Chapter I prohibition in CA98.

Does it contain an excluded restriction? If yes, that restriction is not exempt, but the rest of the agreement may still benefit from the TTBEO and will be enforceable provided that the excluded restriction can be separated from the agreement.

Read Part 4 of the CMA Technology Transfer Guidance for agreements within the scope of the TTBEO, and the TTBEO itself for the legal conditions of the exemption.

Market share thresholds under the TTBEO

The TTBEO uses market share thresholds to identify agreements that are generally less likely to raise competition concerns. These thresholds depend upon whether the parties to the technology transfer agreement are competitors or non-competitors and are set out in the table below.

Relationship between the parties Threshold

Competitors 20% combined market share of the relevant product or technology markets

Non-competitors 30% market share for each party on the relevant product or technology markets

Competitors versus non-competitors

Businesses are competitors if they are active on the same relevant product or technology market and those products or technologies are in the same relevant geographic market.

Product and technology markets

The market share thresholds in the TTBEO apply to each product market and each technology market that is relevant to the technology transfer agreement in question.

A relevant product market is the market for the contract products, in other words the goods or services made using the licensed technology. Identifying the product market involves determining what customers would see as realistic alternatives to those goods or services, based on factors such as price, quality, intended use and availability.

A relevant technology market is the market for the licensed technology itself. Identifying the technology market involves determining whether users of the technology could switch to other technologies that perform the same or a similar function, and whether those technologies are controlled by those who are not party to the technology transfer agreement in question.

Both markets matter because the TTBEO market share thresholds apply both to relevant product markets and relevant technology markets. A licensing agreement may therefore need to be checked against more than one market.

How market shares are calculated

Market shares for the relevant market for the contract products are calculated by looking at the percentage of total sales of the goods or services in question that is accounted for by combining:

the licensee’s sales of any goods or services that it has produced using the licensed technology rights, with

any sales that the licensor has made (if it also supplies products or services using its own technology)

Market shares for the relevant technology market are calculated by looking at the sales of products or services incorporating the licensed technology by the licensor and all licensees, expressed as a percentage of total sales of products or services on the relevant market. The relevant technology market includes both products or services incorporating the licensed technology and competing products or services that incorporate alternative technologies.

Where licensed technology did not generate any sales of contract products in the preceding calendar year, the TTBEO treats that technology as having a 0% market share for that calendar year.

If the market share thresholds are exceeded

If the applicable market-share thresholds are exceeded from the start, the agreement will not benefit from the TTBEO, subject to the alternative technology-market test below.

If the applicable market-share thresholds are satisfied initially and only subsequently exceeded, there is a 3-year grace period following the end of the year in which the threshold was first exceeded. This means that the agreement will benefit from the TTBEO until the end of the 3-year grace period.

Example

A and B are not competitors. They enter into a technology transfer agreement under which A grants B a 20-year exclusive licence to A’s technology.

The applicable market share threshold for each party is 30%.

Neither A nor B sold products incorporating the licensed technology in the preceding calendar year, or anything that would compete with such products. Accordingly, in the first year, each party’s market share is treated as 0%, which is well below the applicable 30% threshold.

The technology proves to be a commercial success. B’s share of the product market is 25% in the second year and rises to 35% in the third year. A’s share of the technology market is 25% in the second year and similarly rises to 35% in the third year. The market share thresholds are therefore exceeded in the third year.

Provided the other conditions of the TTBEO are satisfied, the TTBEO will nevertheless continue to apply to the agreement for a further 3 calendar years following the year in which the threshold was exceeded, that is, until the end of the sixth year.

If the 30% market share threshold is still exceeded by either A or B in the seventh year, the TTBEO will cease to apply to the agreement.

However, this does not mean that the agreement necessarily infringes the Chapter I prohibition. Rather, it will need individual self-assessment.

Since market share thresholds can be difficult to calculate in respect of technology markets, the TTBEO also allows an alternative threshold for licensed technology rights. This involves identifying whether there are at least 3 or more competing technologies in addition to the licensed technology covered by the agreement.

These competing technologies must be both:

independently controlled technologies (that is, ones not controlled by the parties to the agreement in question)

technologies that are regarded by users as interchangeable with the licensed technology

If this test is met, the parties may still benefit from the TTBEO in respect of the technology market, even if the market share thresholds are exceeded in relation to that market.

Read Part 5 of the CMA Technology Transfer Guidance for the market share and other thresholds in the TTBEO, including product markets, technology markets, calculation of market shares and the alternative technology-market test.

Restrictions in technology transfer agreements under the TTBEO: hardcore restrictions and excluded restrictions

Hardcore restrictions

A hardcore restriction is a restriction that is considered to be particularly harmful to competition. If an agreement contains a hardcore restriction, the agreement as a whole will lose the benefit of exemption under the TTBEO.

The hardcore restrictions differ depending on whether the parties are competitors or non-competitors.

Hardcore restrictions between competitors

Competitors: hardcore restrictions What they are

Price fixing Restricting a party’s ability to set its own selling prices.

Output restrictions Limiting how much a party can produce or sell, subject to limited exceptions.

Market or customer allocation Dividing territories or customer groups between the parties.

Restrictions on own technology Preventing the licensee from using, developing or commercialising its own technology rights.

Restrictions on research and development (R&D) Preventing a party from carrying out its own research and development, unless the restriction is needed to protect confidential know-how being disclosed to third parties.

Hardcore restrictions between non-competitors

Non-competitors: hardcore restrictions What they are

Minimum or fixed resale prices Stopping a party from setting its own selling price. Maximum or recommended resale prices may be allowed if they do not amount to fixed prices as a result of pressure from, or incentives offered by, the other party.

Many forms of passive sales restrictions Restricting sales made in response to unsolicited customer requests, general advertising, websites or UK public procurement bids, subject to limited exceptions (for example, passive sales into the exclusive territory or an exclusive customer group reserved for the licensor can be restricted).

Selective distribution restrictions Preventing retailer members of a selective distribution network from selling to end-users, subject to limited exceptions.

Exceptions to the hardcore restrictions

There are exceptions to the hardcore restrictions under the TTBEO for many forms of territorial, customer and production restrictions. The TTBEO allows these because they may be necessary to make licensing arrangements work.

For example, in many situations, it is not a hardcore restriction under the TTBEO for licensors to grant certain forms of exclusive licences in either:

technology transfer agreements between non-competitors

non-reciprocal agreements between competitors

An exclusive licence is one under which the licensor agrees neither to exploit the licensed technology rights itself nor to grant licences to third parties, whether generally or for a particular use or territory. A non-reciprocal agreement is a technology transfer agreement where only one party licenses technology rights to the other, rather than both parties licensing technology rights to each other (or where both parties license each other technology rights but those rights cannot be used to produce competing products).

Example of a non-reciprocal agreement

Company A licenses its technology to Company B. Company B does not license any competing technology back to Company A.

Example of a reciprocal agreement

Company A licenses its technology to Company B. Company B licenses its competing technology to Company A.

It is also not a hardcore restriction under the TTBEO to require the licensee to produce the products with the licensed technology rights only for its own use, provided it remains free to sell such products as spare parts for its own products.

Read Part 6 of the CMA Technology Transfer Guidance for more information about hardcore restrictions under the TTBEO, including the separate rules for agreements between competitors and non-competitors and the exceptions for certain exclusive territories, customer groups and output restrictions.

Example 1 – Hardcore restriction: price fixing between competitors

Company A and Company B are both active in the manufacture and supply of competing products. Each company holds patented technology used for those products and enters into a technology transfer agreement allowing the other party to use its patents. The licensing arrangement provides that products produced using the licensed technologies must be sold for £100 per unit.

Why is this a hardcore restriction?

The parties are actual competitors because they both manufacture and supply competing products. By agreeing the selling price of those products, they restrict their ability to set prices independently.

Example 2 – Hardcore restriction: reciprocal agreement limiting both parties’ output

Company A and Company B are both active in the manufacture and supply of competing products. Each owns competing technology used to make those products, and they license each other their respective patents so that both can manufacture products using features from the other’s technology. The agreement limits each company to producing 50,000 units per year.

Why is this a hardcore restriction?

The parties are actual competitors because they both manufacture and sell competing products.

The respective licences concern competing technologies and can be used to produce competing products, so the arrangement is a reciprocal technology transfer agreement. Limiting the output of both parties reduces the quantity of competing products they can supply.

This would not however be a hardcore restriction in a reciprocal technology transfer agreement if there was only an output restriction on one of the parties.

Example 3 – Hardcore restriction: competing businesses divide markets

Company A and Company B are both active in the manufacture and supply of competing products and each holds technology rights used for those products.

They license each other their competing technologies under a technology transfer agreement that provides that Company A will sell the products only in one territory, while Company B will sell the products only in another territory.

Why is this a hardcore restriction?

The parties are actual competitors because they both sell competing products. By agreeing not to sell in each other’s territories, they allocate markets between themselves. The exception for non-reciprocal agreements does not apply because the parties have granted each other licences concerning competing technologies.

Example 4 – Not a hardcore restriction: exclusive customer groups under a non-reciprocal licence

Company A owns patented technology used in specialist equipment. It licenses the technology to Company B, which uses it to manufacture contract products. Company B does not grant a licence of its own technology to Company A.

Company A reserves one customer group for itself and gives Company B the exclusive right to supply the contract products to a different customer group. The agreement prevents Company A from selling the contract products, actively or passively, to that different customer group.

Why is this not a hardcore restriction under this provision?

This is a non-reciprocal agreement because only Company A grants a technology licence. The restriction protects the exclusive customer group reserved for Company B.

This means Company A may neither actively target the customer group reserved for Company B nor fulfil unsolicited orders from that customer group for the contract products.

Excluded restrictions

An excluded restriction is different from a hardcore restriction. It does not remove the benefit of the TTBEO from the whole agreement, but the restriction itself is not exempt. The rest of the agreement may still be enforceable provided that the excluded restriction can be separated from it.

Excluded restrictions What they are

Exclusive grant backs These are provisions requiring the licensee to transfer ownership of improvements or grant an exclusive licence over improvements to the licensor. Non-exclusive grant back requirements over a licensee’s improvements are permitted under the TTBEO.

No-challenge clauses These are provisions stopping a party from challenging the validity of the other party’s intellectual property rights, with the exception that a licensor can include a provision in an exclusive licence under which it can terminate the licence if the licensee challenges the validity of the licensed technology rights.

Non-competitor own-technology and R&D limits These are restrictions in agreements between non-competitors on the use of the licensee’s own technology or either party’s R&D, unless the restrictions are needed to prevent the disclosure of licensed know-how to third parties.

Read the TTBEO, and Part 7 of the CMA Technology Transfer Guidance, for more information about excluded restrictions under the TTBEO, including exclusive grant-backs, no-challenge clauses and restrictions on a licensee’s own technology or R&D.

Example 1 – Excluded restriction: exclusive grant-back

Company A licenses patented technology to Company B. Company B develops an improved version of that technology. The agreement requires Company B to grant Company A an exclusive licence to that improvement. Company B cannot use the improvement itself or license it to anyone else.

Why is this an excluded restriction?

The obligation requires Company B to give Company A exclusive rights over Company B’s own improvement to the licensed technology. This may reduce Company B’s incentive to invest in further innovation. The exclusive grant-back does not benefit from the block exemption and must be assessed individually. This remains the case even if Company A pays Company B for the exclusive rights, although the payment may be relevant to any individual self-assessment of the agreement.

Example 2 – Not an excluded restriction: non-exclusive grant-back

Company A licenses the same technology to Company B. Company B develops an improvement and must grant Company A a non-exclusive licence to use it. Company B remains free to use the improvement itself and license it to other businesses.

Why is this not an excluded restriction?

Company B does not give up its ability to use or license its improvement. Non-exclusive grant-back obligations are not excluded restrictions under the TTBEO.

Example 3 – Excluded restriction: general ban on challenging UK patents

Company A licenses patents to Company B. The agreement states that Company B must never challenge the validity of Company A’s UK patents.

Why is this an excluded restriction?

The clause prevents Company B from challenging whether Company A’s UK intellectual property rights are valid. Licensees are often well placed to identify invalid rights, and maintaining invalid rights may restrict competition and stifle innovation. The no-challenge clause therefore does not benefit from the block exemption.

Example 4 – Not an excluded restriction: termination of an exclusive licence following a challenge

Company A grants Company B an exclusive licence to its technology. Under the licence, Company A cannot use the technology itself or license it to another business in the relevant field. The agreement allows Company A to terminate the licence if Company B challenges the validity of the licensed UK patents.

Why is this not an excluded restriction?

The clause does not prevent Company B from bringing a challenge. It permits Company A to terminate the agreement if Company B does so. As the licence is exclusive, this termination right is not an excluded restriction under Article 8(3), provided the other TTBEO conditions are met.

Example 5 – excluded restriction: limiting the licensee’s ability to exploit its own technology rights

Company A and Company B are not competitors. Company A licenses its manufacturing technology to Company B. The licence provides that Company B must stop using and licensing its own manufacturing technology and may only use Company A’s technology.

Why is this an excluded restriction?

This restricts the licensee’s ability to exploit its own technology.

Example 6 – excluded restriction: limiting the ability of either party to carry out research and development

Company A and Company B are not competitors. Company A licenses its patented technology to Company B. The licence provides that Company B must not carry out any research or development relating to the technology during the term of the agreement. There is no know-how licensed by the Company A to Company B

Why is this an excluded restriction?

This restricts the licensee’s ability to carry out research and development. There is no know-how licensed to Company B from Company A and the exception in relation to the prevention of disclosure of licensed know-how to third parties is therefore not relevant.

Restrictions benefitting from the TTBEO

There are many restrictions commonly included in technology transfer agreements that are not hardcore restrictions or excluded restrictions. These restrictions may benefit from the TTBEO, provided that the requirements of the TTBEO are otherwise satisfied.

Some examples of these permitted restrictions include the following:

Sole licences

A sole licence is one where the licensor undertakes not to license the technology to third parties within a specified territory, while retaining the right to exploit the licensed technology itself.

Field-of-use restrictions

The licensee can be restricted to particular uses of the technology. For example, a licensee may be allowed to use a technology only for one defined product or service category and not for another.

Quality-control obligations

The licensor can require the licensee to comply with quality standards necessary to protect the value and reputation of the licensed technology or related intellectual property rights.

Read parts 4 to 7 of the CMA Technology Transfer Guidance for further examples of restrictions that may benefit from the block exemption.

If the TTBEO does not apply: individual assessment

If an agreement is not covered by the TTBEO (for example, because the market share thresholds are exceeded or because the agreement involves more than 2 parties), it is not automatically unlawful. It should be assessed individually to see whether they infringe the Chapter I prohibition and, if they do, whether they meet the Section 9 exemption criteria.

However, hardcore restrictions are likely to infringe the Chapter I prohibition and are unlikely to satisfy the exemption criteria.

When assessing an agreement individually, consider whether the restriction is genuinely needed to commercialise or disseminate the technology, and whether consumers receive a fair share of the benefits.

Factors to consider when conducting an individual assessment of a technology transfer agreement include:

the nature and content of the agreement

the market position of the parties

the market position of competitors and buyers

barriers to entry or expansion

how easily customers can switch

whether the market is dynamic and allows rivals to innovate and grow

Read Part 11 of the CMA Technology Transfer Guidance for more information about individual assessment of technology transfer agreements that do not benefit from the TTBEO, including application of the Section 9 exemption criteria under CA98.
